⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page documents how TAK Server is deployed on the OpenDefence Kubernetes platform (pvarki/opendefence-platform): one pod, ten containers — the TAK server split into five JVM services, the takrmapi integration API riding alongside it, and a fleet of raw TCP ports for TAK clients. It is for developers and operators who need to know what actually runs in the app-tak namespace. The platform-generic shape every product integration follows (kraftwerk files, Linkerd identity pinning, the integration API contract) is described in Integration pattern — this page covers only what is TAK-specific.

Pod anatomy

Everything TAK runs in a single pod: Deployment tak-server in namespace app-tak, replicas: 1, strategy Recreate (the old pod is killed before the new one starts), ServiceAccount tak. The manifest is k8s/app-tak/base/resources/tak-server.deployment.yaml.

Three init containers run in order before anything else starts:

# Init container Image What it does
1 certs-handler busybox Runs split-ca.sh, a three-line shell script (one awk one-liner plus two renames) that splits the trust-manager ca-bundle ConfigMap (/ca-bundle/ca-cert.pem) into /ca_public/root_ca.pem and /ca_public/intermediate_ca.pem — TAK's keystore tooling wants individual PEM files, not a concatenated bundle
2 takinit ghcr.io/pvarki/tak-server:5.7.32-260524 Runs /opt/scripts/firstrun_rm.sh: first-run provisioning of the TAK database schema and the Java keystores, using the certificate/keystore passwords from the tak-secrets Secret and the server key material under /le_certs/rasenmaeher
3 takrmapi-prep-dirs busybox Creates /data/persistent/public and /data/persistent/private (the private dir chmod 700) on the takrmapi-data volume so takrmapi starts with the layout it expects

Then seven containers run for the life of the pod. TAK Server 5.x is not a monolith here — the same image is started five times with different start-tak.sh arguments, one JVM service per container:

Container Image Role Memory limit
takconfig ghcr.io/pvarki/tak-server:5.7.32-260524 Configuration service (start-tak.sh config); the container that declares all the raw TCP ports 768Mi
takmsg same Messaging service (messaging) — CoT stream handling 1280Mi
takapi same REST/admin API (api) — the only JVM container with real probes (TCP checks on :8443) 1Gi
takreten same Retention/cleanup service (retention) 512Mi
takplug same Plugin manager (pm) 512Mi
tak-ui-nginx nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:alpine-slim Serves the integration UI files on :8080, reading the ui-files emptyDir that takrmapi writes 32Mi
takrmapi ghcr.io/pvarki/tak-integration:1.13.2-260703 The integration API on :8003 — the piece rmapi talks to 1Gi

Because the five JVM services share one pod, the port declarations sit on takconfig but any container can bind them — they share the pod's network namespace. That is also what makes the takrmapi admin call work: loopback inside the pod reaches takapi directly on :8443.

Memory is tamed by two ConfigMaps: the shared jvm-memory-config (from the k8s/_shared/java-memory-tuning kustomize Component — JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=40.0 -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -Xss512k, plus MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2) and the TAK-local tak-heap-config with per-service heap caps (CONFIG_MAX_HEAP=256, MESSAGING_MAX_HEAP=512, API_MAX_HEAP=256, RETENTION_MAX_HEAP=128, PLUGIN_MANAGER_MAX_HEAP=128). Memory requests equal memory limits on every container (CPU has requests only), so the pod's memory footprint is predictable — a bit over 5Gi of memory all told.

Five PVCs back the pod: tak-data (5Gi, /opt/tak/data), ca-public (1Gi, the split CA PEMs), le-certs (1Gi, mounted at /le_certs — the tak-tls server key material is a Secret projected on top of it at /le_certs/rasenmaeher), shared-tak (1Gi, mounted at /pvarki), and takrmapi-data (1Gi, takrmapi's persistent state). Two emptyDirs round it out: ui-files (written by takrmapi at /ui_files/tak, served read-only by nginx) and update-volume (/opt/tak/webcontent/update).

One meshing detail worth knowing: the pod is Linkerd-injected, but every raw TAK port is excluded from the mesh — only takrmapi traffic goes through the proxy. The annotation says so verbatim:

annotations:
  linkerd.io/inject: enabled
  config.linkerd.io/proxy-await: enabled
  # Only takrmapi via linkerd for the time being
  config.linkerd.io/skip-inbound-ports: "8089,8090,8091,8092,8093,8094,8443,9000,9001,9002"

Certificates

Two cert-manager Certificate resources live in the overlays, and they play very different roles.

The server certificate (Certificate tak → Secret tak-tls) is what TAK presents to clients. Locally it is issued by the internal intermediate-ca-issuer for tak.localmaeher.dev.pvarki.fi (plus tak.localhost); in the cloud overlay it is issued by letsencrypt-http01-production for tak.<domain>. The secret is mounted into the pod as /le_certs/rasenmaeher/privkey.pem and fullchain.pem — file names inherited from the legacy Compose stack — and takinit builds the Java keystores from it on first run.

The admin client certificate (Certificate tak-server-admin, CN tak.<domain>, usages including client auth, issued by the internal intermediate-ca-issuer in both overlays) is how takrmapi authenticates to TAK. It is mounted read-only into the takrmapi container as /data/persistent/public/mtlsclient.pem and /data/persistent/private/mtlsclient.key, and takrmapi presents it when driving the TAK admin REST API at https://127.0.0.1:8443 (env TI_TAK_MESSAGING_API_HOST / TI_TAK_MESSAGING_API_PORT). The manifest comment captures the division of labour: this credential is for the TAK admin API only — rasenmaeher traffic is authenticated by Linkerd, not by this cert.

TAK's own revocation checking is off: TAK_OCSP_ENABLE is "false", so a revoked end-user certificate is still accepted by TAK Server itself on the raw ports. The interim enforcement is the callsign-validity check at the Traefik edge — see the known limitation in Edge mTLS & callsign checks.

Database

TAK gets its own CloudNativePG cluster, tak-postgres — the platform's PostGIS holdout: imageName: ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgis:15-3.4, while newer clusters on the platform run PostgreSQL 18 (a commented-out postgis:18-3.6-system-trixie line in the manifest marks the parked upgrade). instances: 1, 5Gi storage, ssl_min_protocol_version: "TLSv1.2".

Bootstrap creates database tak owned by role tak, and postInitApplicationSQL (copied, per the in-file comment, from the legacy stack's pg_init/03_tak.sh) creates the postgis and pgcrypto extensions. A CNPG Database CR named tak-postgres additionally declares the full extension set TAK wants:

Extension Purpose
postgis Spatial types and functions
postgis_topology Topology model
fuzzystrmatch Fuzzy string matching (geocoder dependency)
postgis_tiger_geocoder TIGER geocoder

All TAK containers get their connection details (POSTGRES_DB, POSTGRES_ADDRESS, POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD) from the operator-generated tak-postgres-app Secret — the standard pattern described in Data & secrets. Like every database on the platform, tak-postgres runs a single instance with no backups configured.

Admin automation

takrmapi is the TAK integration API — the component that implements the platform's integration contract (healthcheck, user lifecycle hooks, client instruction packages) and translates rmapi's orchestration calls into TAK admin REST calls. rmapi reaches it in-cluster at http://tak-server.app-tak.svc.cluster.local:8003/ (from the kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init product registry), and takrmapi accepts those calls only from rmapi's pinned Linkerd identity (certcn in the pod's kraftwerk-init.json, plus MTLS_TRUST_L5D=true). What happens when rmapi provisions a TAK user:

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
    participant rmapi
    participant takrmapi
    participant takapi
    participant ldap as OpenLDAP
    rmapi->>takrmapi: user lifecycle call to tak-server.app-tak:8003 (plain HTTP)
    Note over rmapi,takrmapi: Linkerd wraps the hop in mesh mTLS - takrmapi accepts only the pinned rmapi identity
    takrmapi->>takapi: TAK admin REST call to https://127.0.0.1:8443 inside the pod
    Note over takrmapi,takapi: takrmapi presents the tak-server-admin CLIENT certificate (mtlsclient.pem + key)
    takapi->>ldap: LDAP bind to openldap.opendefence-system:1389
    ldap-->>takapi: user and group data
    takapi-->>takrmapi: admin API response
    takrmapi-->>rmapi: provisioning result

blocks.html:
The LDAP leg exists because TAK is configured against the platform's OpenLDAP (LDAP_URL=ldap://openldap.opendefence-system.svc.cluster.local:1389). The bind credentials cross a namespace boundary to get there: the tak-secrets ExternalSecret uses a Kubernetes-provider SecretStore (tak-keycloak-secrets) authenticating as ServiceAccount tak-ldap-secret-reader to read LDAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD out of the keycloak-ldap-admin Secret in opendefence-system. The same ExternalSecret also generates the TAK keystore passwords (takserver-cert-pass, tak-ca-pass) with the password-32-8digits-no-symbols generator. This cross-namespace reader pattern is covered in Data & secrets.

Startup is slow by design: takrmapi's startupProbe allows up to ten minutes (60 × 10s against /api/v1/healthcheck on :8003) because it polls the TAK API and runs first-boot default setup before it reports healthy — expect the pod to take minutes to go Ready after a deploy.

Network exposure

TAK is reachable in two very different ways, and only one of them goes through Traefik.

HTTPS via Traefik — three IngressRoutes on the websecure entrypoint, all with TLS options mtls-optional (client certificate verified if presented):

IngressRoute Match Middlewares Backend
tak tak.<domain> + /api mtls-chain-with-legacy (pass client cert → callsign-validity check against rmapi → redirect/403 on failure → legacy DN headers) tak-server service, port 8003 (takrmapi)
tak-ephemeral tak.<domain> + /ephemeral/api mtls-legacy-client-cert-headers only — no callsign chain on this enrollment-time path tak-server service, port 8003
tak-ui mtls.<domain> + /ui/tak none beyond the entrypoint defaults tak-server service, port 8080 (tak-ui-nginx)

Raw TCP, bypassing Traefik entirely — the tak-server-external Service exposes the TAK protocol ports straight to clients. TLS and client-certificate authentication on these ports is TAK Server's own, using the keystores takinit built:

Port Purpose
8089 CoT streaming / config
8443 Secure API (client cert)
9000 / 9001 / 9002 Federation v1 / v2 / auth
8090–8094 Data feeds 1–5

Locally this Service is a NodePort with each nodePort equal to the real port number (the kind cluster widens service-node-port-range to 1024–9999 and binds these ports on 127.0.0.1 via extraPortMappings); in the cloud it is a LoadBalancer with allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false. The in-cluster tak-server ClusterIP Service carries the same TAK ports plus 8003 (takrmapi, for rmapi and Traefik) and 8080 (the UI).

Honest rough edges

  • Eight health checks are stubs. The liveness and readiness probes on takconfig, takmsg, takreten and takplug (2 × 4 = 8) are literally:

livenessProbe:
  exec:
    command: ["true"] # FIXME: Implement proper health check

They can never fail, so Kubernetes cannot detect or restart a wedged JVM in those four containers. Only takapi (TCP probes on :8443), tak-ui-nginx and takrmapi (HTTP probes) have real checks.

  • Single replica, **Recreate** strategy — every update or reschedule means downtime for all connected TAK clients.
  • **tak-postgres** is one instance with no backups, like every database on the platform.
  • The managed **tak** database role has **superuser: true** — inherited from the legacy stack's provisioning, broader than TAK needs.
  • PostgreSQL is pinned to PostGIS 15-3.4 while the rest of the platform has moved to 18; the upgrade is visibly parked in a comment.
  • The JVM containers and **takrmapi** run as root (runAsUser: 0); only tak-ui-nginx runs unprivileged with all capabilities dropped.
  • OCSP is disabled (TAK_OCSP_ENABLE "false"), so certificate revocation is enforced only at the Traefik edge, not on the raw TCP ports.
